name: System Justification
description: People are motivated to see existing institutions, hierarchies, and arrangements as legitimate and fair, even when those arrangements disadvantage them. That motive can make the status quo feel natural, deserved, or harder to challenge than it objectively is.
design_relevance_note: Useful in civic-tech, service design, org tooling, and fairness work: teams can end up optimizing around today's workflow or policy because it feels legitimate, rather than questioning whether the underlying system is itself biased or exclusionary.
prevalence_note: Common in social and political psychology, and sometimes explicit in design-justice/civic-tech practice, but far less common as a named concept in mainstream product-design pattern libraries or CRO-style UX discourse.

findings.description: Across a decade of work summarized in the review, system justification theory argues that people are motivated to see the existing social order as legitimate and fair, sometimes even when doing so conflicts with their personal or group interest; the review integrates evidence across 20 hypotheses, including implicit outgroup favoritism among disadvantaged groups.
findings.source_title: A Decade of System Justification Theory: Accumulated Evidence of Conscious and Unconscious Bolstering of the Status Quo

findings.description: Four experiments found that exposure to complementary stereotype pairings (e.g., 'poor but happy'/'rich but miserable', 'poor but honest'/'rich but dishonest') increased explicit system-justification scores and implicitly activated justice-related concepts on a reaction-time task, relative to noncomplementary stereotype exposure. A distinct, direct experimental demonstration of a system-justification mechanism (complementary stereotyping as a specific psychological pathway), independent of and closing the single-study-risk gap left by the existing integrative review (Jost, Banaji & Nosek 2004), which synthesizes findings rather than reporting its own new experiments.
findings.source_title: Complementary Justice: Effects of "Poor but Happy" and "Poor but Honest" Stereotype Exemplars on System Justification and Implicit Activation of the Justice Motive
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
